blocks.text: Part 1 · DBMS Complete Notes
{icon:database} **1. What is a Database?** A ==database== is a collection of related data that is stored, organized and maintained so it can be easily __accessed, managed and updated__.

**2. What is DBMS?** A ==DBMS== is software that lets users define, create, maintain and control access to databases. It sits as an __interface__ between users or applications and the physical database.

**3. What is RDBMS?** A ==Relational DBMS== stores data as tables (relations) built from rows (__tuples__) and columns (__attributes__). It uses ==SQL== (Structured Query Language) to manipulate and manage the data.

items: **5. Advantages of DBMS:** reduced data ==redundancy==
improved data consistency

blocks.text: DBMS Notes · Part 1 Fundamentals
The ==relational model== is the most widely used data model in DBMS. It represents data as __tables__ (relations).

spec.caption: top row = Attributes (Columns) · v rows = Tuples (Rows)

items: **2. Tuple (Row):** each row in a relation
represents a single ==record== or entity
**3. Attribute (Column):** each column in a relation
represents a ==property== of an entity
**5. Degree (Arity):** number of attributes (columns)
table with 6 columns has degree **6**
**4. Domain:** set of all possible values of an attribute
example Age → {0, 1, 2, …, 120}
**6. Cardinality:** number of tuples (rows)
table with 150 rows has cardinality **150**
**7. Relational Schema:** blueprint / structure of a relation
notation `Relation_Name(Attribute1, ..., AttributeN)`

blocks.title: ☆ Key Takeaway
items: relational model is ==simple== and structured
it is the __foundation of RDBMS__
**8. NULL** = missing, unknown or not-applicable value
NULL is **not** zero and not an empty string
**2. Candidate Key:** a ==minimal== super key
no proper subset can still identify a tuple
Example: STUDENT candidates = {Roll_No}, {Email}, {Aadhaar_No}

blocks.text: DBMS Notes · Part 1 Fundamentals
A ==key== is an attribute or set of attributes that can __uniquely identify a tuple__ (row) in a relation.

items: **1. Super Key:** any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple
a relation can have ==many== super keys
Example: STUDENT(Roll_No, Email, Aadhaar_No, Name, Dept)
{Roll_No}, {Email}, {Aadhaar_No}, {Roll_No, Email}, {Roll_No, Name}, {Email, Name} …
**3. Primary Key:** one candidate key chosen to identify each tuple
cannot hold **NULL** values
Example: choose Roll_No, each student uniquely identified
**4. Alternate Key:** candidate keys __not__ chosen as primary
Example: Roll_No is PK, so Email and Aadhaar_No are alternate
**5. Foreign Key:** attribute in one relation referring to the PK of another
maintains ==referential integrity==
Example: ENROLLMENT.Roll_No references STUDENT(Roll_No)
**6. Composite Key:** two or more attributes combined
used when no single attribute is unique
Example: ENROLLMENT(Roll_No, Course_ID) is composite

DBMS Notes · Part 1 Fundamentals
==Normalization== is a systematic way to organize table data to __reduce redundancy__ and avoid __update anomalies__.

items: **1. Functional Dependency:** X → Y means X uniquely determines Y
Y is functionally dependent on X, written `X -> Y`
Example STUDENT: Roll_No → Name, Age, Dept
Example: Dept → Dept_Name

rows: unique row id; NOT NULL + UNIQUE

blocks.title: 2. Referential Integrity
items: FK value ==must exist== in the referenced table
prevents invalid / orphan data
on update or delete: **RESTRICT** blocks, **CASCADE** propagates
**SET NULL** sets FK to NULL, **SET DEFAULT** sets FK default

cards.title: (a) One-to-One 1:1
lines: each A row ↔ at most one B row
EMPLOYEE(Emp_ID PK, Name, Email, Passport_ID FK UNIQUE)

cards.title: (b) One-to-Many 1:N
lines: one A row ↔ many B rows
one dept has many students; each student one dept

cards.title: (c) Many-to-Many M:N
lines: many A rows ↔ many B rows via ==junction== table
STUDENT(Roll_No PK, Name, Email) · COURSE(Course_ID PK, Course_Name)
student takes many courses; course has many students

blocks.title: Key Rule
items: two rows with the ==same X== must have the ==same Y==

rows: cannot add a fact without an unrelated fact
same data in many rows, edits inconsistent
deleting a row loses other data
delete last CSE student, lose Dept_Phone

blocks.title: Types of Functional Dependency
items: **Trivial:** Y ⊆ X, e.g. Roll_No, Name → Roll_No
**Non-trivial:** Y ⊄ X, e.g. Roll_No → Name
**Fully functional:** Y depends on the __whole__ of X
**Partial:** Y depends on part of a composite key
**Transitive:** Y depends on X through another attribute Z
**3. 1NF Rule 1:** all attributes hold ==atomic== (indivisible) values
**Rule 2:** each column holds values of the same domain
**Rule 3:** each row is unique, use a primary key

tables.title: After 1NF
tables.caption: Atomic now: every phone × skill pair; ==4NF== removes this redundancy

items: **4. 2NF:** must be in ==1NF== first; no **partial dependency**
every non-key attribute fully depends on the whole primary key
Below, key is (Roll_No, Subject_ID): Subject_Name depends only on Subject_ID
Student_Name depends only on Roll_No, so {red:partial dependency}
After 2NF split, all non-key attributes are ==fully dependent==
**1. 3NF:** must be in ==2NF==; no **transitive dependency**
non-key attributes depend __only__ on the primary key
Example: ENROLLMENT(Roll_No, Student_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name, Dept_Location)
FDs: Roll_No → Student_Name, Dept_ID · Dept_ID → Dept_Name, Dept_Location

blocks.text: DBMS Notes · Part 1 Fundamentals
Higher normal forms remove ==transitive==, ==multi-valued== and ==join== dependencies.

items: **1. Concept:** may read, update, insert or delete data
treated as a ==single unit== of execution
either **all** operations succeed or **none** do

tables.title: Enrollment (3NF)
tables.caption: no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute

items: **2. BCNF:** stronger 3NF; for every FD X → Y, X must be a ==super key==
fixes anomalies from **overlapping candidate keys**
Example: TEACHING(Teacher_ID, Course_ID, Course_Name), key = both
FD Course_ID → Course_Name; determinant is **not** a super key ⇒ not BCNF
split into TEACHING1(Teacher_ID, Course_ID) and COURSE(Course_ID, Course_Name)

tables.title: TEACHING (not BCNF)
tables.caption: Course_ID → Course_Name but Course_ID is not a super key

tables.title: TEACHING1
tables.caption: every determinant is a super key

tables.title: COURSE
tables.caption: BCNF removes anomalies due to multiple candidate keys

items: **3. 4NF:** must be in ==BCNF==; no non-trivial **multi-valued dependency**
removes redundancy from independent multi-valued facts
Example: STUDENT_HOBBY_LANG(Roll_No, Hobby, Language)
MVDs: Roll_No ->> Hobby · Roll_No ->> Language (independent)

blocks.text: DBMS Notes · Part 1 Fundamentals
A ==transaction== is a logical unit of work that must be completed __entirely__ or __not at all__.

items: **Mistakes:** splitting with no shared attribute → {red:lossy join}
over-normalizing = many joins, ==slower reads==
BCNF can **lose** an FD; a 3NF split always keeps them

blocks.title: Example (Bank Transfer)
items: transfer Rs 1000 from Account A to B
step 1: debit 1000 from A
step 2: credit 1000 to B
both must succeed, else ==roll back==

tables.title: STUDENT_HOBBY
tables.caption: Hobby and Language stored separately, no redundancy

items: **4. 5NF (PJNF):** must be in ==4NF==; no non-trivial **join dependency**
cannot decompose further without losing information
Example: SPJ(Supplier, Part, Project) with JD *(Supplier, Part, Project)
==Cycle rule==: S supplies P · P used in J · S supplies J ⇒ S supplies P for J
so SPJ = the three-way join of SP, SJ, PJ; **no two-way** split is lossless

tables.title: SJ
tables.caption: joining SP, SJ, PJ recreates SPJ without spurious tuples

blocks.title: 5. Lossless Join & Dependency Preservation
items: **Lossless join:** rejoin tables without losing or adding tuples
**Dependency preservation:** every FD stays checkable after the split
**Goal:** less redundancy and fewer anomalies, data still recoverable

rows: every X is a super key

items: **4. Commands:** `COMMIT` saves all changes permanently
`ROLLBACK` undoes all changes of the transaction
`SAVEPOINT` marks a point inside a transaction
`ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` undoes changes after that point
`RELEASE SAVEPOINT` removes a savepoint

blocks.note: rollback to sp1 also destroys sp2

blocks.title: ☆ Savepoint Rule
blocks.text: `ROLLBACK TO sp1` ==destroys every savepoint created after sp1==. A later `RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp2` then **fails** — MySQL raises `ERROR 1305: SAVEPOINT sp2 does not exist`; PostgreSQL and Oracle behave the same.

rows: credit B fails, debit A rolled back
two transfers at once don't clash

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes changes ==after that point only== :)

blocks.note: SQL steps: both updates, then COMMIT

items: **Mistakes:** no `COMMIT` — work is unsaved and still holds ==locks==
`ROLLBACK` after a commit undoes **nothing**
DDL (`CREATE`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`) auto-commits in MySQL / Oracle

blocks.title: ☆ Key Rule
blocks.text: Nothing is permanent until ==COMMIT== — and once committed, even a **crash** cannot undo it.
